chunks: From him, from al-Qasim and Fadalah, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Isa ibn Abdillah al-Qummi, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I shoot an arrow and do not know if I said the name of God (bismillah) or not.' He said: 'Eat it, there is no harm.' I said: 'I shoot and it gets lost, and I find my arrow inside it.' He said: 'Eat it, provided that part of it has not been eaten; if part of it has been eaten, then do not eat from it.'

key_terms.سَمَّيْتُ: I named (recited the name of God)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating game shot with an arrow if I am unsure if I said Bismillah?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) applies the principle of *istishab* (presumption of continuity) to resolve the doubt regarding the recitation of *bismillah*, deeming the game permissible. The ruling further distinguishes between the meat and the arrow itself, prohibiting consumption if the prey ingested the arrow, thereby linking the physical state of the prey to the validity of the hunt. This narration highlights the practical application of doubt in Shia jurisprudence, emphasizing that minor uncertainties do not invalidate the primary act of slaughter.
